questions.q: In SSMS, what is the quickest way to start a new profiling query against a database?
options: Right-click the server or database in Object Explorer and choose New Query
Edit the table's data directly in Object Explorer
Open Windows Notepad and save the file as .sql
Restart the SQL Server service
questions.explain: Right-clicking a server or database and choosing New Query opens a fresh Query Editor tab pointed at that database — the starting point for every profiling query in this lesson.

questions.q: If COUNT(*) returns 10,000 but COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) returns 9,850 on a table where CustomerID should be unique, what does this most likely indicate?
options: There are likely duplicate CustomerID values — a uniqueness problem
The table has exactly 150 NULL rows
The query has a syntax error
CustomerID is not a valid column name
questions.explain: When total row count exceeds the distinct count of a column meant to be unique, that gap typically signals duplicate values — the uniqueness dimension from Lesson 2/15.

questions.q: What does the pattern SUM(CASE WHEN EmailAddress IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) calculate?
options: The count of rows where EmailAddress is NULL
The count of rows where EmailAddress is NOT NULL
The average length of the EmailAddress column
The number of distinct email addresses
questions.explain: This CASE expression returns 1 for each NULL row and 0 otherwise, so SUM() totals up exactly the NULL count for that column.

questions.q: Why does this lesson's percentage calculation use 100.0 instead of 100 when computing a NULL rate?
options: Because T-SQL's integer division would otherwise truncate the decimal result to zero
Because 100.0 runs faster than 100 in SQL Server
Because SSMS requires decimal literals in all SELECT statements
There's no actual difference between 100 and 100.0 in T-SQL
questions.explain: Using 100 (an integer) with integer division would silently truncate the percentage to zero; 100.0 forces decimal division so the real percentage is returned.

questions.q: Per this lesson, do the SSMS screenshots (New Query, Execute, Results grid) show the literal output of the exact profiling queries in this lesson?
options: No — they show SSMS's general query workflow, since the mechanics are identical regardless of which query is run
Yes — they are a live capture of the exact COUNT(DISTINCT) query shown in this lesson
Yes — SSMS was run live in this course's sandbox to produce them
No — they are AI-generated mockups of the SSMS interface
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that these are real, official Microsoft screenshots of SSMS's general workflow, honestly captioned, not claimed as the literal output of this lesson's specific queries.
